Qawmi and Jamaat: Leaders and Their Online Support Brigades in the Arena of Criticism!

Mutual criticism between followers of the Qawmi and Jamaat traditions is nothing new. Rather, it has become almost an everyday reality.

As a matter of principle, however, I do not consider criticism inherently negative. On the contrary, constructive, evidence-based, and respectful criticism can serve as an effective means of self-examination and self-correction for individuals, organizations, and intellectual traditions alike.

But when such criticism degenerates into personal attacks, hostile language, or verbal abuse, it ceases to be an exchange of views and instead creates new grounds for division and animosity.

Based on my observations over a considerable period, one particular aspect has struck me as especially noteworthy.

There appears to be little fundamental difference between the conduct of ordinary supporters on either side, including those often referred to as their respective 'bot brigades'.

On social media, the language used by some of these individuals is often excessively emotional, sharp, vulgar, and, at times, aggressive. In many instances, the tendency to defeat or humiliate opponents is far more evident than any inclination towards reasoned dialogue.

The reality is that the leaders of these organizations cannot always effectively control the statements and conduct of such informal online supporters. Consequently, many of their comments emerge as expressions of personal emotions and impulsive reactions.

My observations, however, are somewhat different when it comes to the leadership.

In my assessment, many of the senior and influential leaders of Jamaat tend to adopt a comparatively restrained position, even when subjected to harsh criticism from the Qawmi circles. They often choose to remain silent; and even when they respond, their reactions are generally expressed in relatively measured and controlled language.

On the other hand, in my observation, criticism of Jamaat and its leaders by some senior figures and respected elders from the Qawmi circles tends to be comparatively sharper, more caustic, distasteful, and, at times, openly aggressive.

Of course, I am not claiming that this observation applies equally to every individual or institution. Rather, it represents my personal assessment based on publicly expressed statements and discussions over an extended period.

In reality, leadership plays an extremely important role in shaping the language and conduct of the followers of any organization or intellectual tradition. When leaders set examples of restraint, courtesy, fairness, and reasoned criticism, the likelihood of these values taking root among their followers increases considerably.

Conversely, when the statements of leaders become excessively emotional, distasteful, provocative, or confrontational, their influence is often reflected in the language and behaviour of their followers as well.

Differences of opinion are inevitable—that is a reality of intellectual and social life. What matters most, however, is that such differences must never cross the boundaries of mutual respect, moral courtesy, and Islamic *Akhlaq* (ethical conduct).

Therefore, irrespective of differences in organizational or ideological affiliations, the language of every leader should be refined, responsible, and constructive. Mutual criticism, in turn, should be evidence-based, rational, and conducted with decorum.

**Note:** By 'bot brigades', I do not mean the official representatives of either organization. Rather, the term refers to certain excessively active and aggressive supporters on social media.
